etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English line, lyne, from Old English līne (“line, cable, rope, hawser, series, row, rule, direction”), from Proto-West Germanic *līnā, from Proto-Germanic *līnǭ (“line, rope, flaxen cord, thread”), from Proto-Germanic *līną (“flax, linen”), from Proto-Indo-European *līno- (“flax”). Influenced in Middle English by Middle French ligne (“line”), from Latin linea. More at linen.

The oldest sense of the word is “rope, cord, thread”; from this the senses “path”, “continuous mark” were derived.

definitions.definition: (geometry) An infinitely extending one-dimensional figure that has no curvature; one that has length but not breadth or thickness.
(geometry, informal) A line segment; a continuous finite segment of such a figure.
(graph theory) An edge of a graph.
(geography) A circle of latitude or of longitude, as represented on a map.
(geography, 'the line' or 'equinoctial line') The equator.
(music) One of the straight horizontal and parallel prolonged strokes on and between which the notes are placed.
(cricket) The horizontal path of a ball towards the batsman (see also length).
(soccer) The goal line.

quote.citation: 2011 October 1, Clive Lindsay, “Kilmarnock 1-2 St Johnstone”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: St Johnstone's Liam Craig had to clear off the line before Steven Anderson sent a looping header into his own net for the equaliser on 36 minutes.

definitions.definition: (automotive) A particular path taken by a vehicle when driving a bend or corner in the road.

quote.citation: 2021 February, The Road Ahead, Brisbane, page 10, column 3:
quote.text: "I guess it's like race cars - if you get the right line you can come out at top speed."

definitions.definition: A path through two or more points (compare ‘segment’); a continuous mark, including as made by a pen; any path, curved or straight.
A rope, cord, string, or thread, of any thickness.
A hose or pipe, of any size.
Direction, path.
A procession, either physical or conceptual, which results from the application or effect of a given rationale or other controlling principles of belief, opinion, practice, or phenomenon.
The wire connecting one telegraphic station with another, a telephone or internet cable between two points: a telephone or network connection.
A clothesline.

quote.citation: 1985, Joan Morrison, Share House Blues, Boolarong Publications, page 26:
quote.text: She feels guilty for pampering him, and salves her conscience by bossily ordering him to go and fetch the clothes from the line[.]

definitions.definition: A letter, a written form of communication.
A connected series of public conveyances, as a roadbed or railway track; and hence, an established arrangement for forwarding merchandise, etc.
(especially military) A trench or rampart, or the non-physical demarcation of the extent of the territory occupied by specified forces.
The exterior limit of a figure or territory: a boundary, contour, or outline; a demarcation.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, Paradise Lost, volume IV:
quote.text: Eden stretch'd her Line / From Auran Eastward to the Royal Towrs / Of great Seleucia,

definitions.definition: A long tape or ribbon marked with units for measuring; a tape measure.
(obsolete) A measuring line or cord.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Isaiah 44:13:
quote.text: The carpenter stretcheth out his rule; he marketh it out with a line; he fitteth it with planes, and he marketh it out with the compass, and maketh it after the figure of a man, according to the beauty of a man; that it may remain in the house.

definitions.definition: That which was measured by a line, such as a field or any piece of land set apart; hence, allotted place of abode.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 16:6:
quote.text: The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.

definitions.definition: A threadlike crease or wrinkle marking the face, hand, or body; hence, a characteristic mark.
Lineament; feature; figure (of one's body).
(military, nautical) Ellipsis of line of battle.

A more-or-less straight sequence of people, objects, etc., either arranged as a queue or column and often waiting to be processed or dealt with, or arranged abreast of one another in a row (and contrasted with a column), as in a military formation. [from mid-16th c.]

quote.citation: 1817, Percy Shelley, The Revolt of Islam:
quote.text: A band of brothers gathering round me, made, / Although unarmed, a steadfast front […] now the line / Of war extended, to our rallying cry / As myriads flocked in love and brotherhood to die.

definitions.definition: (military) The regular infantry of an army, as distinguished from militia, guards, volunteer corps, cavalry, artillery, etc.
(music) A series of notes forming a certain part (such as the bass or melody) of a greater work.

quote.citation: 2015, Mícheál Houlahan, Philip Tacka, Kodály in the Third Grade Classroom:
quote.text: Students and the instructor sing the harmony line while the instructor plays the melody line on the piano.

definitions.definition: A series or succession of ancestors or descendants of a given person; a family or race; compare lineage.
A written or printed row of letters, words, numbers, or other text, especially a row of words extending across a page or column, or a blank in place of such text.
A verse (in poetry).

quote.citation: 1609, William Shakespeare, Sonnet 71:
quote.text: Nay if you read this line, remember not, / The hand that writ it.

definitions.definition: A sentence of dialogue, especially [from late 19th c.] in a play, movie, or the like.

quote.citation: 2010, Alison Hodge, Actor training, page 138:
quote.text: Anyone who has worked with Littlewood will wince at the memory of going over single lines time and time again, each actor in turn speaking the line until the valid intonation, phasing and emphasis emerged.

definitions.definition: A lie or exaggeration, especially one told to gain another's approval or prevent losing it.
A small amount of text. Specifically:
Course of conduct, thought, occupation, or policy; method of argument; department of industry, trade, or intellectual activity. [from earlier 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1823 April 27, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, “Kean—Sir James Mackintosh—Sir H. Davy—Robert Smith [Robert Percy Smith?]—Canning—National Debt—Poor Laws”, in H[enry] N[elson] C[oleridge], editor, Specimens of the Table Talk of the Late Samuel Taylor Coleridge. […], volume I, London: John Murray, […], published 1835, →OCLC, page 25:
quote.text: He [Mackintosh] is uncommonly powerful in his own line; but it is not the line of a first-rate man.

definitions.definition: The official, stated position (or set of positions) of an individual or group, particularly a political or religious faction. [from later 19th c.]
(slang) Information about or understanding of something. (Mostly restricted to the expressions get a line on, have a line on, and give a line on.)

quote.citation: 1916 March 11, Charles E. Van Loan, “His Folks”, in Saturday Evening Post‎[1]:
quote.text: She's got the best line on Hickey. Maybe she knows a way to put the heart back into him.

definitions.definition: A set of products or services sold by a business, or by extension, the business itself. [from early 19th c.]

quote.citation: 1890, Illinois State Dairymen's Association, Annual Report (volume 16, page 21)
quote.text: Have nothing to do with snide goods; let it be known throughout the world that the farmers and dairymen, yea, and those engaged in other industries in the great State of Illinois, produce only the best of everything in their lines, and we will be the last to feel the effects of over-production.

definitions.definition: (stock exchange) A number of shares taken by a jobber.
(historical) A tsarist-era Russian unit of measure, approximately equal to one tenth of an English inch, used especially when measuring the calibre of firearms.
One twelfth of an inch.

quote.citation: 1883, Alfred Swaine Taylor, Thomas Stevenson, The principles and practice of medical jurisprudence:
quote.text: The cut is measured in thickness from a quarter of a line to a line and a half (a line is one-twelfth of an inch).

definitions.definition: One sixteenth of an inch.
One fortieth of an inch.

quote.citation: 1922, “Statement of James Turner, Representing Universal Button Fastening Co., Detriot, Mich.”, in Hearings Before the Committee on Finance, United States Senate, page 5337:
quote.text: In case any of the committee do not understand what is meant by a rate per line, I may say that buttons, being very small, are not measured by the foot or inch, but by the line, a line being one-fortieth of an inch. For example, that is a 27-line button […].

definitions.definition: Any of an ill-defined set of units of length, varying according to the country, discipline, industry, and date of application, commonly with no indication of the intended magnitude:

quote.citation: 1847, Sir Erasmus Wilson, On Diseases of the Skin. Second edition:
quote.text: Withof estimates that the hair of the beard grows one line (French) in the course of a week, let us call it one line and a half (Engish); this would amount to six inches and a half yearly...

definitions.definition: (advertising) Short for agate line.

quote.citation: 1912, Miscellaneous Series, numbers 7-11, page 25:
quote.text: Advertising rates, line contract, less than 500 agate lines, 12 cents per line; 1,000 to 2,000 lines, 7 cents; 5,000 to 10,000 lines, 5 cents.

definitions.definition: (historical) A maxwell, a unit of magnetic flux.
(baseball, slang, 1800s, with "the") The batter's box.
(fencing) The position in which the fencers hold their swords.

quote.citation: 1861, George Chapman, Foil Practice, with a Review of the Art of Fencing, page 12:
quote.text: Thus, for example, in the line of Quarte, the direct thrust is parried by dropping the point under the adversary's blade and circling upwards, throwing off the attack in the opposite line (that of Tierce), and upon the direct thrust in the line of Tierce, by a similar action throwing off the attack in the opposite line (that of Quarte).

definitions.definition: (engineering) Proper relative position or adjustment (of parts, not as to design or proportion, but with reference to smooth working).
(informal) A small path-shaped portion or serving of a powdery illegal drug, especially cocaine.
(obsolete) Instruction; doctrine.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalms 19:4:
quote.text: Their line is gone out through all the earth, and their words to the end of the world. In them hath he set a tabernacle for the sun.

definitions.definition: (genetics) A population of cells derived from a single cell and containing the same genetic makeup.
(perfusion line) a set composed of a spike, a drip chamber, a clamp, a Y-injection site, a three-way stopcock and a catheter.
(ice hockey) A group of forwards that play together.

(Australian rules football) A set of positions in a team which play in a similar position on the field; in a traditional team, consisting of three players and acting as one of six such sets in the team.
(medicine, colloquial) A vascular catheter.
(transitive) To place (objects) into a line (usually used with "up"); to form into a line; to align.
(transitive) To place persons or things along the side of for security or defense; to strengthen by adding; to fortify.

quote.citation: 1599, William Shakespeare, Henry V, ii 4:
quote.text: Line and new repair our towns of war With men of courage and with means defendant.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To form a line along.
(transitive) To mark with a line or lines; to cover with lines.
(rail transport) To align (one or more switches) to direct a train onto a particular track.
(transitive, obsolete) To represent by lines; to delineate; to portray.

quote.citation: 1598, William Shakespeare, As You Like It, iii 2:
quote.text: All the pictures fairest lined Are but black to Rosalind.

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated, now more often line out) To read or repeat line by line.
(intransitive, baseball) To hit a line drive; to hit a line drive which is caught for an out. Compare fly and ground.
(transitive) To track (wild bees) to their nest by following their line of flight.
(transitive) To measure.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Korean 라인 (rain, “members with a shared characteristic”), itself from English line. Likely generalized via hyung line, maknae line, etc.

definitions.definition: (South Korean idol fandom) A group of people born in a certain year (liners).

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Old English līn (“flax, linen, cloth”). For more information, see the entry linen.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Flax; linen, particularly the longer fiber of flax.
(transitive) To cover the inner surface of (something), originally especially with linen.

quote.citation: 1922, E[ric] R[ücker] Eddison, The Worm Ouroboros‎[3], London: Jonathan Cape, page 19:
quote.text: In the midst stalked the King, his great limbs muffled, like Goldry’s, in a cloak: and it was of black silk lined with black bearskin, and ornamented with crabs worked in diamonds.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To fill or supply (something), as a purse with money.

quote.citation: 1602, Richard Carew, edited by Thomas Tonkin, Carew's Survey of Cornwall‎[4], published 1811, page 34:
quote.text: because the charge amounteth mostly very high for any one man's purse, except lined beyond ordinary, to reach unto

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Middle French ligner.

definitions.definition: (transitive, now rare, of a dog) To copulate with, to impregnate.
